scenes.animation: Zippy stands at a school canteen counter comparing two cartoon managers. Manager A decides the menu instantly alone. Manager B holds a vote, posts the menu on a noticeboard and takes a while. Zippy taps his foot at Manager B.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Manager A decides in two seconds. Manager B takes a whole week. Isn't A better?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Faster is not always better. Let's see how we should assess what democracy actually delivers.

scenes.animation: A report card titled 'Outcomes of Democracy' lists subjects: 'Accountable, responsive, legitimate government', 'Economic growth and development', 'Reduction of inequality and poverty', 'Accommodation of social diversity', 'Dignity and freedom of citizens'. A caption: 'Democracy is better than other forms of government'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracy promotes equality among citizens, enhances the dignity of the individual, improves the quality of decision making, provides a method to resolve conflicts, and allows room to correct mistakes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But democracy is only a form of government. It can create conditions for achieving something, and citizens have to take advantage of those conditions.

scenes.animation: Manager B's noticeboard enlarges: 'Rules followed', 'Decision process open', 'Any student can check'. Label 'Transparency'. A timer shows 'Takes more time', then a second label pops up 'Better, more acceptable decisions'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The most basic outcome is an accountable government. It is responsible to the citizens and responsive to their needs and expectations.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A democratic government may take more time, because it follows procedures and negotiations. But its decisions are more acceptable to people and more effective.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracy ensures that decision making is based on norms and procedures. So a citizen has the right and the means to examine the process of decision making. This is known as transparency.

scenes.animation: A checklist of things democracies do: regular, free and fair elections; open public debate on major policies; citizens' right to information. Some items tick; others show a half-filled circle. Then a giant stamp lands: 'Legitimate: people's own government'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracies regularly hold free and fair elections, open public debate, and give citizens a right to information about the government. On these, the record is not perfect but better than non-democratic regimes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democratic governments often frustrate the needs of people and ignore demands of a majority. Corruption also exists. But there is nothing to show that non-democracies are less corrupt.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democratic government is legitimate. It may be slow, less efficient and not always responsive, but it is people's own government. People wish to be ruled by representatives elected by them.

scenes.animation: A 'Board Tip' sticker lands on the word 'Transparency' with its definition highlighted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: define transparency, and explain why democracy is called a legitimate government. Both are common short answers.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a canteen noticeboard icon. Points appear: '1. Accountable and responsive', '2. Transparent: citizens can examine decisions', '3. Legitimate: people's own government'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: democracy produces an accountable and responsive government.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: it may be slower, but it is transparent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: its greatest strength is that it is legitimate, the people's own government.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Manager B, my vote is yours. Take your week.

scenes.animation: Two cartoon race cars on a track labelled '1950 to 2000'. One car is a dictator in a crown, the other carries a crowd waving a ballot. The dictator's car edges slightly ahead at the finish line. Zippy gasps.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The dictator won the growth race! Does that mean dictatorships are better?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hold on. The lead is small, and the race isn't the whole story.

scenes.animation: A bar chart titled 'Rates of economic growth, 1950 to 2000' builds: a bar for 'Dictatorships' slightly taller than a bar for 'Democracies'. A second pair of bars, 'Poor countries under dictatorship' and 'Poor countries under democracy', is almost the same height, with a label 'Negligible difference'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If we consider all democracies and all dictatorships for the fifty years between 1950 and 2000, dictatorships have a slightly higher rate of economic growth.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But when we compare their record only in poor countries, the difference in growth rates almost disappears.

scenes.animation: A flowchart builds: 'Economic development depends on' branches into 'Population size', 'Global situation', 'Cooperation from other countries', 'Economic priorities of the country'. A small 'Form of government' box sits beside, marked 'Not the only factor'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Economic development depends on several factors: the country's population size, the global situation, cooperation from other countries, and economic priorities adopted by the country.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the inability of democracy to achieve higher economic development worries us. But this alone cannot be a reason to reject democracy.

scenes.animation: A scale weighs 'Slightly lower growth' against a heavy pile of positives: 'Accountable', 'Legitimate', 'Dignity', 'Freedom'. The scale tips clearly in democracy's favour.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So why not pick the faster car?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because the difference is small, and democracy has several other positive outcomes. It is better to prefer democracy, even if it does not guarantee the fastest growth.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Even if democracies do not guarantee economic development, we can expect democracy not to lag behind dictatorships in this respect.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: a common question asks whether dictatorships are better for economic growth. Say the difference is slight, negligible for poor countries, and that growth depends on many factors besides the form of government.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a race car icon. Points appear: '1. Dictatorships: slightly higher growth, 1950 to 2000', '2. Among poor countries: negligible difference', '3. Growth depends on many factors'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: from 1950 to 2000, dictatorships showed slightly higher economic growth.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: among poor countries, the difference is negligible.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: growth depends on population, the global situation, cooperation and priorities, not just the form of government.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm sticking with the car full of voters. It's more fun anyway.

scenes.animation: An election booth: a rich man in a suit and a daily-wage worker each drop exactly one ballot into the box. Zippy grins. Then the camera pans to their homes: a mansion and a small hut.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Same vote, same power. So they're equal, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Politically, yes. Economically, not quite. That's one of democracy's biggest challenges.

scenes.animation: A label 'Political equality: one person, one vote' glows. Beside it, a ladder shows a small group at the top holding a large sack labelled 'Share of national income', and a large crowd at the bottom with small coins. A caption: 'Economic inequalities growing'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracies are based on political equality. All individuals have equal weight in electing representatives.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But alongside political equality, we find growing economic inequalities. A small number of ultra-rich enjoy a highly disproportionate share of wealth and incomes, while those at the bottom have very little to depend upon.

scenes.animation: A question mark hovers over a ballot box: 'Poor voters are a large proportion. Why don't parties prioritise poverty?' Then a thought bubble shows basic needs: food, clothing, house, education, health.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: But the poor are a big part of the voters. Won't every party rush to help them?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That is what we would expect. The poor constitute a large proportion of our voters, and no party will like to lose their votes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yet democratically elected governments do not appear to be as keen to address the question of poverty as you would expect them to.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In actual life, democracies do not appear to be very successful in reducing economic inequalities. Many people in poorer democracies still struggle to meet basic needs of life, such as food, clothing, house, education and health.

scenes.animation: A split card: left side 'Democracy guarantees: political equality' in green; right side 'Democracy has not guaranteed: economic equality' in amber. A 'Board Tip' sticker lands between them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the record is mixed. Democracy has given people equal political rights, but it has not been as successful in reducing poverty and economic inequality.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: when asked whether democracy reduces economic inequality, answer honestly. Explain political equality first, then the growing economic inequality.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a one-vote icon. Points appear: '1. Political equality: one person, one vote', '2. Economic inequalities growing', '3. Poverty not addressed as expected'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: democracy is based on political equality, one person, one vote.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: yet economic inequalities are growing in many democracies.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: democratic governments have not addressed poverty as keenly as expected.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Equal votes. Now let's work on equal chances.

scenes.animation: A school cricket team picks players only from one group while others watch. Then the scene resets: the whole class plays together, taking turns to captain. A scoreboard reads 'Harmony: 1, Conflict: 0'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why does the whole class play better when everyone gets a turn?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because no group feels shut out. Democracy works the same way with social diversity.

scenes.animation: Two condition cards appear: 'Majority rule is not rule by majority community' and 'Majority must work with minority', then 'Everyone must get a chance to be in the majority at some point'. A small Belgium map glows green beside a Sri Lanka map in grey for contrast.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracies usually develop a procedure to conduct their competition. This reduces the possibility of tensions becoming explosive or violent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion. The majority always needs to work with the minority so that governments represent the general view.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Also, rule by majority does not become rule by majority community in terms of religion, race or linguistic group. Every citizen should have a chance of being in the majority at some point of time.

scenes.animation: Two cartoon groups step forward, a woman holding a placard 'Equal respect' and a Dalit activist holding a placard 'Equal status'. Their placards glow brighter as the word 'Democracy' shines behind them. A caption reads 'Wrong and unjust, not just unequal'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracy stands much superior to any other form of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The long struggles by women have created some sensitivity today that respect and equal treatment of women are necessary ingredients of a democratic society. In a democracy, discrimination against women can be claimed as wrong and unjust, with public and legal backing.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Democracy in India has also strengthened the claims of the disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity.

scenes.animation: A bar marked 'Expectations' keeps rising as people ask for more. A label 'Complaints are a testimony to success' flashes. The subjects become citizens holding placards and questioning leaders.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: But people complain about democracy all the time!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That itself is a sign of success. As people get some benefits, they ask for more. The fact that people are complaining is a testimony to the success of democracy. It shows people have become subjects-turned-citizens, able to examine those in power.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: questions on how democracy accommodates diversity and ensures dignity of women and disadvantaged castes are frequently asked.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a cricket team icon. Points appear: '1. Majority works with minority', '2. Dignity of women and disadvantaged castes', '3. Complaints = sign of success'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: democracy accommodates diversity when the majority works with the minority.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: it promotes the dignity and freedom of women and disadvantaged castes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: rising expectations and complaints show democracy's success.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next match, I'm captain. Democratically elected, of course.
